docs.title: systemspec-credential
docs.text:
A registry of credentials without their values: what each one is for, where and how it is generated, what it is entitled to do, where it is stored, who uses it, who owns it, and how it rotates. An event log records when each was created, rotated, deployed, verified, given an expiry or revoked. From the two, credspec works out where every credential stands, writes reports for people and documentation sites, and fails a deploy script when something is expired or overdue.

It is both a management tool and documentation: the registry says what should exist, the log says what happened, and the reports show what to do next.

docs.title: What It Answers
docs.text:
• What credentials do we have? Every secret, key, token, certificate and account, per system and environment, in one validated file.
  • Who does what? Whether a person or a system generates, distributes and rotates each one, and how many need you by hand.
  • What do I do next? Each credential is to-create, to-record, to-deploy or deployed, with its next step: the console or command that makes it and how to install it in each store.
  • What is due? A lifecycle state from the rotation policy and the events: ok, due, overdue, expiring, expired and more, and a calendar of every rotation and expiry.
  • What does a leak expose? reaches and dependsOn link credentials, so each shows everything its holder can get and which others expose it.

docs.title: No Values
docs.text:
No type has a field for a value, and no command reads one. Values stay in their stores: a cloud parameter store, a secrets manager, CI secrets or a password manager. The registry records where they are.

Keep reports private

Reports hold no values, but they list where every credential is stored and what it can reach, which is as sensitive as an inventory. Keep them with the registry, in a private repository, not on a public site.

docs.title: Part of the SystemSpec Family
docs.text: systemspec-credential is one of a family of Go-first specifications, each describing one aspect of a system as validated JSON with generated schemas: architecture, cryptography, design systems, API style, pricing and credentials. Each stands alone, and they refer to one another by ID rather than by importing each other.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go install github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/cmd/credspec@latest

The core packages, credspec and report, depend only on the standard library and oscompat, which has no dependencies of its own.

docs.title: Events, Work and States
docs.text: The registry says what should exist. The event log says what happened. From the two, each credential gets a work progress (what to do next) and a lifecycle state (whether it is due).

docs.title: The Event Log
docs.text:
events.json is an append-only list. Each event names a credential, a type and a time at, with optional expires, by and note.

Type Meaning expires created The first value exists Optional rotated A new value replaced the old one Optional expires The issuer set or changed the expiry Required deployed The value is in place in its rendered stores Not allowed verified Someone confirmed the value is present and works Not allowed revoked The value no longer works Not allowed

A created or rotated event without expires clears any earlier expiry, because the new value has none.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
credspec record example-app/prod/SESSION_KEY created --by ops
credspec record example-app/ci/MODULES_TOKEN rotated --expires 2027-05-01 --by admin
credspec record 'example-app/prod/*' deployed --by deploy
credspec record example-org/github-owner verified --note "hardware key checked"
  • --at records something that happened earlier, as a date or an RFC 3339 time; the default is now.
  • * in the ID matches any text, slashes included, so one command records every match.
  • The log is kept sorted by time, then credential, then type, so it diffs cleanly in version control.

Only credspec record needs to touch the file; it validates each event against the registry before writing.

docs.title: Work Progress
docs.text:
Progress says where the work on a credential stands. It drives the HTML report's default order, the plan's checklists and status --progress.

Progress When Next step to-create Planned, with no created or rotated event Create it: the console or command, then install it in each store to-record Active, so it exists, but nothing is recorded Record it as created, with --at the date it was made to-deploy It has a rendered store and no deployed event since it last changed Deploy it, then record deployed deployed Created, and deployed since; or no rendered store Nothing retired Status retired, or a revoked event Nothing

A rotation sends a credential back to to-deploy until the next deployed event. A federated credential has no value: it counts as created once deployed.

credspec status --progress to-create,to-record --manual

lists what you, rather than a system, still have to make or record.

docs.title: Lifecycle States
docs.text:
The state says whether a credential needs attention now. The first state that applies wins:

State When retired Status retired, or a revoked event planned Planned, and not created yet unrecorded Active, with no created or rotated event expired The expiry has passed overdue Scheduled, and the last change plus the interval has passed expiring The expiry is within the warning window due Scheduled, and the rotation date is within the warning window unknown-expiry Rotates on expiry, with no expiry recorded ok Otherwise

The warning window is 30 days; --warn-days changes it. A planned credential with a created event is assessed like an active one, so you can create credentials ahead of a launch.

docs.title: Using status as a Gate
docs.text:
status exits non-zero when any credential is in a --fail-on state, expired,overdue by default:

credspec status                          # fail on expired or overdue
credspec status --fail-on expired,overdue,expiring
credspec status --fail-on ''             # list only, never fail

Filter with --system, --env, --state and --progress, or pass --all to list every credential.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This guide installs credspec, runs it over the example registry, and then walks through the loop you repeat for real credentials: declare, create, record, deploy, report.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: go install github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/cmd/credspec@latest

docs.title: Try the Example
docs.text:
The repository's examples/basic holds a registry of six credentials for an imaginary example-app, and an event log:

cd examples/basic
credspec validate
credspec status --as-of 2026-06-01

credspec reads credentials.json and events.json from the current directory unless you pass --registry and --events. --as-of fixes the date so the output matches this page:

WORK       STATE       CREDENTIAL                    OWNER             BY HAND                     REASON
deployed   overdue     example-app/prod/DB_PASSWORD  platform team     generate,rotate             rotation was due 2026-03-01
to-record  unrecorded  example-org/github-owner      repository admin  generate,distribute,rotate  active, but no created or rotated event
2 of 6 credentials listed, as of 2026-06-01
Error: 1 credential(s) expired or overdue

status lists what needs attention and exits non-zero when anything is expired or overdue, which makes it a gate for deploy scripts and CI.

docs.title: Write a Registry
docs.text:
A registry is a JSON file listing credentials. One entry is one secret in one place for one environment. This is the smallest useful entry:

{
  "$schema": "https://github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/schema/registry.schema.json",
  "formatVersion": "1",
  "credentials": [
    {
      "id": "example-app/prod/SESSION_KEY",
      "name": "SESSION_KEY",
      "system": "example-app",
      "environment": "prod",
      "kind": "random-secret",
      "status": "planned",
      "owner": "platform team",
      "issuer": { "type": "self" },
      "generation": { "method": "random", "command": "openssl rand -hex 32" },
      "stores": [
        { "type": "aws-ssm", "role": "primary", "path": "/example/prod/SESSION_KEY" }
      ],
      "rotation": { "policy": "scheduled", "intervalDays": 180 },
      "handling": { "generate": "human", "distribute": "system", "rotate": "human" }
    }
  ]
}

The $schema line gives editors completion and checking. credspec schema registry writes the same schema to a file. The Registry describes every field, including the ones that make the reports useful: where to create the value, how to install it in each store, what it is entitled to do and what its leak exposes.

docs.title: The Loop
docs.text:
1. Declare each credential before it exists, with status: planned. credspec status --progress to-create lists what is still to make.
  2. Create it, following its generation command or console steps, straight into its primary store.

  3. Record that it exists:

    credspec record example-app/prod/SESSION_KEY created --by ops

    Then change its status to active.

  4. Deploy it where its consumers read it, and record that too. A pattern records many at once:

    credspec record 'example-app/prod/*' deployed --by deploy

  5. Report and repeat. credspec status in CI catches what comes due; credspec report writes the HTML report, the plan and the calendar.

Events, Work and States explains how events turn into work and states.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Write the HTML report and open it: credspec report -o credentials.html. See Reports.
  • With many systems and environments, build the registry in Go so one function makes each environment's entries. See Using It from Go.

docs.title: Using It from Go
docs.text: The registry can be a JSON file, but with several systems and environments it is easier to build in Go: one function makes each environment's entries, so staging and production cannot drift apart. The same validation applies either way.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Purpose Dependencies credspec Types, validation, event log, states, progress, reach Standard library and oscompat report HTML, Markdown, plan, calendar and JSON reports Standard library and oscompat schema The JSON Schemas, generated from the types and embedded invopop/jsonschema cli The commands as a Cobra command you can mount Cobra 
go get github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential

docs.title: Building a Registry
docs.text:
import "github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/credspec"

func sessionKey(env string) credspec.Credential {
    return credspec.Credential{
        ID:          "example-app/" + env + "/SESSION_KEY",
        Name:        "SESSION_KEY",
        System:      "example-app",
        Environment: env,
        Kind:        credspec.KindRandomSecret,
        Status:      credspec.StatusActive,
        Owner:       "platform team",
        Issuer:      credspec.Issuer{Type: credspec.IssuerSelf},
        Generation:  credspec.Generation{Method: credspec.MethodRandom, Command: "openssl rand -hex 32"},
        Stores: []credspec.Store{{
            Type: credspec.StoreAWSSSM, Role: credspec.RolePrimary,
            Path: "/example/" + env + "/SESSION_KEY",
        }},
        Rotation: credspec.Rotation{Policy: credspec.PolicyScheduled, IntervalDays: 180},
        Handling: credspec.Handling{
            Generate: credspec.ActorHuman, Distribute: credspec.ActorSystem, Rotate: credspec.ActorHuman,
        },
    }
}

func Registry() (*credspec.Registry, error) {
    reg := credspec.NewRegistry()
    for _, env := range []string{"staging", "prod"} {
        reg.Add(sessionKey(env))
    }
    return reg, reg.Validate()
}

Validate returns every problem at once, each with its entry's ID. A test that calls Registry() keeps the registry valid in CI.

Other entry points:

  • LoadRegistry and ReadRegistry read JSON, refusing unknown fields.
  • LoadLog reads the event log and checks it against the registry; a missing file is an empty log.
  • Assess and ProgressOf give one credential's state and progress from its record (log.Record(id)).
  • Exposes and ExposedBy follow dependsOn and reaches.

docs.title: Mounting the Commands
docs.text:
cli.New returns the whole command tree, validate, status, report, record, export and schema, over a registry your code builds:

import "github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/cli"

root.AddCommand(cli.New(cli.Options{
    Use:        "credentials",
    Title:      "Example credentials",
    Registry:   Registry,
    EventsPath: "credentials/events.json",
}))

Your tool then has mytool credentials status, mytool credentials record … and the rest. With Registry set, there is no --registry flag. export writes the Go-built registry as JSON, for other tools and for the schema-aware editors.

docs.title: Writing Reports
docs.text:
import "github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/report"

rep := report.Build("Example credentials", reg, log, time.Now(), credspec.DefaultWarn)
err := rep.HTML(w)
err = rep.Plan(w, reg, report.PlanOptions{EnvironmentOrder: []string{"prod", "staging"}})
err = rep.Calendar(w, report.CalendarOptions{})
err = report.Markdown(w, "Example credentials", reg)

docs.title: Checking Committed Reports
docs.text:
Commit the reports next to the registry and let a test fail when one is out of date. The page records its own date, so the test rebuilds it for that date and compares:

func TestReportCurrent(t *testing.T) {
    reg, err := Registry()
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    log, err := credspec.LoadLog("credentials/events.json", reg)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    page, err := os.ReadFile("credentials/credentials.html")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    asOf, err := report.AsOf(page)
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    var b bytes.Buffer
    if err := report.Build("Example credentials", reg, log, asOf, credspec.DefaultWarn).HTML(&b); err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    if !bytes.Equal(b.Bytes(), page) {
        t.Error("credentials.html is out of date: regenerate the reports")
    }
}

The Markdown reference needs no date: rebuild it from the registry alone and compare.

docs.title: The Registry
docs.text: The registry lists every credential a set of systems needs, without values. It validates against rules that are the same whether you write JSON or build it in Go, and its JSON Schema is generated from the Go types.

docs.title: One Entry per Secret, Place and Environment
docs.text: The staging and production copies of a key are two entries, because they are created, stored and rotated separately. IDs are stable and unique, conventionally system/environment/NAME, using letters, digits and ._/:@-.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text: Field Required Meaning id yes Stable, unique ID name yes Display name, often the variable or parameter name description What it is for system yes The system that owns it environment prod, staging and so on; empty for one shared by every environment kind yes What it is; see Kinds status yes planned, active or retired sensitivity low, medium, high or critical owner yes The person or role who creates and rotates it tags, links Free labels, and title plus url links

docs.title: Where It Comes From
docs.text:
issuer is who issues the value: type (such as self, aws, github), account, and console, the URL where a person manages it.

generation is how the value is made:

Field Meaning method random, keypair, issued (by the issuer), derived (built from others, listed in dependsOn) or federated (no stored value) spec The shape, such as "32 random bytes, hex" where Where it is made, such as "the operator's machine, straight into the parameter store" command The command that makes it steps Console steps, in order, when there is no command

docs.title: Where It Lives and Who Uses It
docs.text:
stores lists every place the value is kept. Each has a type (such as aws-ssm, github-actions, password-manager, host-file), a path, an account, a console and a role:

Role Meaning primary The source of truth. Every credential needs one, unless federated backup An offline copy, such as in a password manager rendered Written from the primary at deploy time, where consumers read it

install says, in a sentence or a command, how the value gets into that store. The reports put it in each credential's next step, so write it for the person who will do it.

consumers lists who reads it: system, component, and via, such as env SESSION_KEY.

docs.title: What It Can Do
docs.text:
Field Meaning entitlements What the issuer grants it: resource, access, note, such as a token's scopes exposure What a holder of the value can do, in a sentence revocation How to revoke it quickly dependsOn IDs it is built from, such as a connection string from a password reaches IDs a holder of this one can read, use or replace, such as every parameter an AWS identity can read

dependsOn and reaches together let each report show what a leak exposes in all, following links through other credentials, and which credentials expose this one.

docs.title: Rotation and Handling
docs.text:
rotation says when the value is replaced:

Policy Meaning scheduled Every intervalDays on-expiry Before the issuer's expiry, recorded with an expires event on-demand Only on compromise or need

procedure and impact describe how a rotation is done and what it interrupts.

handling says who does each stage, human or system:

Stage Meaning generate Makes the value distribute Gets it from its primary store to its consumers rotate Replaces it

automation names the systems doing the system stages. The reports count how many credentials need a person for at least one stage, how many are fully automatic, and how many rotations a person does in a year.

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text: A person's login that controls other credentials, such as the owner of a code-hosting organization or a cloud root user, is an entry of kind account. Give it protections (such as "hardware security key", "MFA") and recovery (how to regain access, or that it cannot be), and list in reaches what it controls. The plan lists every account's protections, and a verified event ticks them off.

docs.title: Kinds
docs.text:
kind, issuer.type and stores[].type are open sets: any lowercase slug is valid, and these are the well-known values the reports and the schema suggest.

  • kind: random-secret, password, private-key, certificate, connection-string, oauth-client, api-token, personal-access-token, access-key, encryption-key, ssh-key, federated, account.
  • issuer type: self, aws, cloudflare, github, google-cloud, postgres, stripe, registrar.
  • store type: aws-ssm, aws-secrets-manager, aws-kms, github-actions, password-manager, pulumi-config, host-file, local-file, none.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
credspec validate reports every problem at once, each with its entry's ID:

  • required fields are present and IDs are unique;
  • closed sets hold only their values, and open sets are slugs;
  • every credential has a primary store, unless federated;
  • scheduled has intervalDays above zero, and other policies have none;
  • dependsOn and reaches name existing IDs, never the entry itself;
  • link and console URLs are absolute https URLs.

A registry file refuses unknown fields, so a misspelled field is an error rather than silently ignored.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
credspec report writes five formats from the same rows: each credential, its record, its state, its progress and next step, its history, and what its leak exposes.

credspec report --format html     -o credentials.html
credspec report --format markdown -o reference.md
credspec report --format plan     -o plan.md
credspec report --format ics      -o credentials.ics
credspec report --format json     -o report.json

Keep reports private

No report holds a value, but each lists where every credential is stored and what it can reach. Keep them with the registry, in a private repository, not on a public site.

docs.title: HTML Report
docs.text:
One self-contained file that makes no network requests. It opens sorted by work progress, so what you have to do comes first.

  • Search over IDs, names, descriptions and paths.
  • Filters for work, system, environment, kind, state, issuer, store, consumer, owner, sensitivity, rotation, who generates, distributes and rotates, and tag.
  • Chips count each kind of work within the other filters; the "you create" chip shows only what a person makes by hand.
  • Details for every credential: each attribute, its next step, what it exposes and what exposes it, and its history.
  • CSV download of the rows shown.

Filters live in the URL's fragment, so a link opens the same view. For example, credentials.html#progress=to-create&generate=human shows what you create by hand, and #tag=launch the credentials tagged launch.

docs.title: Markdown Reference
docs.text:
A page for a documentation site: a "by hand, by place" checklist of what a person creates, grouped by issuer and account, then a section per system with every credential's details and how to install it in each store.

It depends only on the registry, never on the time or the events, so a test can regenerate it and fail when the committed copy is out of date.

docs.title: Management Plan
docs.text:
The plan, in Markdown, answers "what do I do, and when":

  1. Summary: counts by status, system and environment, state, work and who does each stage, and the rotations a person does in a year.
  2. Launch checklist: what a person creates, in the order to do it: accounts first, then shared credentials, then each environment and its systems, each credential after those it is built from. Each item has its console, command, where to install it and the command that records it.
  3. To record and to deploy: credentials waiting for an event.
  4. Rotation calendar: every rotation and expiry in the next 12 months.
  5. Account protections, ticked by verified events.
  6. Exposure: the credentials whose leak exposes the most, and what cannot be recovered, with its backup.

Order the checklist with --environment-order prod,staging and --system-order shared,api,web, and change the calendar's horizon with --months.

docs.title: Calendar
docs.text:
An iCalendar (RFC 5545) file with an all-day event for each scheduled rotation, repeating at its interval, and each expiry. Each event has a reminder before it (--remind-days, by default the warning window) and the procedure, impact, console and record command in its description. Late items are placed on the report's date.

Event IDs are stable, so importing a newer file updates the same events rather than adding copies.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text: The rows with their records, states and progress, for other tools.

docs.title: Committing Reports
docs.text:
The HTML report, the plan and the calendar depend on the date, so each records the date it was assessed: a meta element, a comment or an X-CREDSPEC-AS-OF property. The time is taken at the start of the day (UTC).

To check a committed copy is current, read its date with report.AsOf, rebuild it with --as-of that date, and compare. Using It from Go shows the test.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Each release has its own notes. The full changelog, generated from CHANGELOG.json, is CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Version Date Highlights v0.1.0 2026-11-01 Credential registry without values, work progress and lifecycle states, HTML report, management plan and calendar

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
The first release of systemspec-credential: a registry of the credentials a set of systems needs, without their values, and an event log of what happened to each. From the two, credspec works out what to do next and what is due, and writes it out for people.

  • One validated registry. Every secret, key, token, certificate and account: what it is for, how and where it is made, what it may do, where it is stored, who uses it, who handles it and how it rotates. Write it in JSON or build it in Go; both pass the same validation, and the JSON Schemas are generated from the Go types.
  • What to do next. Each credential is to-create, to-record, to-deploy or deployed, with its next step: the console or command that makes it, and how to install it in each store.
  • What is due. A lifecycle state from the rotation policy and the events, and a status command that fails a deploy when anything is expired or overdue.
  • Reports for people. A self-contained HTML report, a management plan with the launch checklist and the rotation calendar, an iCalendar export and a Markdown reference for documentation sites.

docs.title: The Registry
docs.text:
Each entry describes one credential in one place for one environment.

  • Where it comes from: the issuer and its console, and the generation method (random, keypair, issued, derived or federated) with the command or console steps.
  • Where it lives: each store with its role (primary, backup or rendered), path, console, and how the value is installed there.
  • Who uses it and what it may do: consumers, entitlements, what a holder can do and how to revoke it.
  • Rotation: scheduled, on-expiry or on-demand, with the procedure and its impact.
  • Handling: whether a person or a system generates, distributes and rotates it. Every report counts what needs you by hand.
  • Reach: dependsOn and reaches link credentials, so each shows what its leak exposes, directly or through others, and which credentials expose it.
  • Accounts: a person's login that controls other credentials, with its protections and recovery.

See The Registry.

docs.title: Events, Work and States
docs.text:
credspec record adds created, rotated, expires, deployed, verified and revoked events, for one credential or every one matching a * pattern. From them come each credential's work progress and its lifecycle state: ok, due, overdue, expiring, expired, unknown-expiry, unrecorded, planned or retired.

See Events, Work and States.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
Format For html Browsing: search, filters, details, shareable filtered views, CSV plan Doing: the launch checklist in dependency order, what to record and deploy, the rotation calendar, account protections, exposure ics Remembering: every rotation and expiry with a reminder, stable across re-imports markdown Documentation: a reference that depends only on the registry json Other tools

Time-dependent reports record their as-of date, read back by report.AsOf, so a test can check a committed copy is current. See Reports.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Purpose credspec Types, validation, event log, states, progress, reach report The reports schema The generated JSON Schemas, embedded cli The commands, mountable in your own Cobra tool cmd/credspec The standalone command

credspec and report depend only on the standard library and oscompat. Files are written atomically, and the same code is correct on Linux, macOS and Windows. See Using It from Go.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
go install github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential/cmd/credspec@v0.1.0

or, as a library:

go get github.com/plexusone/systemspec-credential@v0.1.0

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: This is the first release. The registry and event log formats are at formatVersion 1; a change that breaks existing files will change that version.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• A MkDocs site with guides to getting started, the registry, events and states, reports and use from Go.
  • The product and technical requirements, the plan and the roadmap under Design.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Build the library first, then the reports, then the command line over them, so a host tool can use each layer on its own. Each phase ends with a usable release.

Phase Delivers Release 1. Registry Types, validation, event log, state, JSON, schemas v0.1.0 with phase 2 2. Reports and command line HTML, Markdown and JSON reports; the mountable commands; the standalone command v0.1.0 3. Observed state An observer interface and checks for missing, unlisted and expired credentials; observers for a cloud parameter store and CI secrets v0.2.0 4. Lifecycle automation Random values generated into a store; rotation reminders; findings as OCSF events; an MCP server v0.3.0

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
• No values, ever. Keeping values out of the model keeps the registry safe to version and review, and leaves storage to the tools built for it.
  • One entry per secret, place and environment. Flat entries are simple to filter and to assess. Go code removes the repetition.
  • Events, not dates in the registry. Definitions change when intent changes; events change when an operator acts. Keeping them apart keeps the registry reviewable and the history auditable.
  • Open sets for kinds, issuers and stores. New services appear all the time; a slug is enough to filter on. Closed sets are kept for the values the code acts on.
  • The Markdown reference is independent of time, so a committed copy can be tested for currency; the HTML report includes state and is generated on demand.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation The registry drifts from the stores Phase 3 compares them; until then the event log and verified events Operators forget to record events unrecorded is a state of its own, shown first The report leaks an inventory It holds no values; it is kept beside the registry, never published

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A deployment creates credentials faster than anyone keeps track of them: signing keys, session keys, database passwords, OAuth clients, CI tokens, cloud access keys, origin certificates. Each lives in a different place, was made a different way, can do different things and has its own expiry or rotation schedule. The knowledge of what exists, why, and when it must change ends up spread across runbooks, console screens and memory. Then a token expires and CI breaks, a key is never rotated, or a leaked credential cannot be revoked quickly because nobody knows what it can reach or what breaks when it changes.

Secret stores hold values, but each sees only its own secrets, and none records intent: what a credential is for, how to make it, what it may do, who uses it, and how it must be rotated.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Operators who deploy and run systems and must create, rotate and revoke their credentials.
  • Reviewers (security, privacy, audit) who need a complete, current list of credentials and what each can reach.
  • Tooling (deploy checks, CI) that must refuse to proceed when a credential is expired or overdue.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One registry of every credential, without values. Each entry records what it is, where it is generated and how, what it is entitled to do, where it is stored, who uses it and through what, who owns it, how it rotates, what breaks when it does, and how to revoke it.
  2. Defined in Go code or JSON. A team that already writes its infrastructure in Go builds the registry in Go, so one loop over its systems and environments produces their entries. Others write JSON. Both validate against the same rules, and the JSON Schema is generated from the Go types.
  3. Lifecycle state. An append-only event log records when each credential was created, rotated, verified, given an expiry or revoked. From it and the registry, each credential has a state: ok, rotation due, overdue, expiring, expired, unrecorded, planned or retired.
  4. A report people use. A single, self-contained HTML file to search and filter by name, system, environment, kind, issuer, store, consumer, owner, rotation state and expiry, with every attribute and the history of each credential. A Markdown reference for documentation sites. JSON for other tools.
  5. A gate. A command that exits non-zero when any credential is in a chosen state, such as expired or overdue, for deploy scripts and CI.
  6. Embeddable. The command line is a library: a host tool mounts the same commands over its own Go-defined registry.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Storing or reading secret values. systemspec-credential never holds a value. Stores such as a cloud parameter store, a secrets manager or a password manager do.
  • Issuing credentials at their issuer (GitHub, a cloud provider) in the first releases. Generation is documented, and later automated for random values only.
  • A hosted service. The first releases are a library and a command line over files kept in version control.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: # Requirement Priority R1 A credential entry with the attributes in goal 1 Must R2 Validation: unique IDs, required fields, known values for closed sets, references to other entries resolve Must R3 Load and save a registry and an event log as JSON with stable formatting Must R4 JSON Schemas generated from the Go types Must R5 State from the registry, the events and a point in time, with a warning window Must R6 Self-contained HTML report with search, filters, sorting and details Must R7 Markdown reference that depends only on the registry, so it can be checked for currency Must R8 A command line: validate, status (with a failing gate), report, record an event, export, schema Must R9 The command line as a mountable Cobra command over any registry source Must R10 Observe stores to find missing, unlisted and expired credentials Later R11 Generate random values straight into a store Later R12 Findings as OCSF events Later

docs.title: Success Measures
docs.text:
• Every credential a deployment needs is in the registry before it is created, and the report is the first place an operator looks.
  • No credential expires or passes its rotation date unnoticed: the gate catches it first.
  • A leaked credential's reach, consumers and revocation steps are known from one entry.

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text:
One Credential is one secret in one place for one environment: the staging and production copies of a key are two entries. Go code builds both from one function.

Field Type Notes id string Stable and unique, such as example-app/prod/SESSION_KEY. Letters, digits and ._/:@- name string Display name, often the variable or parameter name description string What it is for system string The system that owns it environment string prod, staging and so on; empty for one shared by every environment kind slug Well-known values listed below; others allowed status enum planned, active, retired sensitivity enum low, medium, high, critical owner string A person or role who creates and rotates it issuer object type (slug), account, console (URL) generation object method (enum), spec, where, command, steps entitlements list resource, access, note stores list type (slug), role (enum), account, path, console (URL), install (how the value gets there), note consumers list system, component, via, note rotation object policy (enum), intervalDays, procedure, impact handling object generate, distribute, rotate (each human or system), automation revocation string How to revoke it quickly exposure string What a holder of the value can do dependsOn list IDs this one is derived from, such as a DSN from a password reaches list IDs a holder of this one can read, use or replace protections list What guards it besides secrecy, such as MFA recovery string How to regain access when it is lost, or that it cannot be tags list Free labels links list title, url

Well-known values (open sets, validated as lowercase slugs):

  • kind: random-secret, password, private-key, certificate, connection-string, oauth-client, api-token, personal-access-token, access-key, encryption-key, ssh-key, federated, account (a person's login that controls other credentials).
  • issuer type: self, aws, cloudflare, github, google-cloud, postgres, stripe, registrar.
  • store type: aws-ssm, aws-secrets-manager, aws-kms, github-actions, password-manager, pulumi-config, host-file, local-file, none.

Closed sets:

  • generation method: random, keypair, issued, derived, federated.
  • store role: primary (the source of truth), backup (an offline copy), rendered (written from the primary at deploy time).
  • rotation policy: scheduled (every intervalDays), on-expiry (before the issuer's expiry), on-demand (only on compromise or need).
  • actor, for each handling stage: human (a person, by hand) or system. generate makes the value, distribute gets it from its primary store to its consumers, rotate replaces it. automation names the systems doing the system stages.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• id, name, system, kind, status, owner, generation.method, rotation.policy and each handling stage are required; IDs are unique.
  • Closed sets hold only their values; open sets are slugs.
  • At least one store with role primary, unless the method is federated.
  • scheduled requires intervalDays > 0; other policies forbid it.
  • dependsOn and reaches name existing IDs and never the entry itself.
  • Link and console URLs are absolute https URLs.
  • All problems are reported together, each with the entry's ID.

docs.title: Event Log
docs.text:
An append-only JSON list of events: credential (an ID), type, at, optional expires, by and note.

Type Meaning expires created The first value exists Optional rotated A new value replaced the old one Optional expires The issuer set or changed the expiry Required deployed The value is in place in its rendered stores, where consumers read it Not allowed verified Someone confirmed the value is present and works Not allowed revoked The value no longer works Not allowed

Events name known IDs. Append keeps the log sorted by time, then credential, then type, so saving is stable. A credential's record is the latest of each: created, rotated (or created), expiry, verified, revoked. A created or rotated event without expires clears the expiry.

docs.title: Progress
docs.text:
Separate from the state, ProgressOf says where the work on a credential stands:

Progress When to-create Not active (planned) and no created or rotated event; a federated one: no deployed event to-record Active, so it exists, but no created or rotated event to-deploy It has a rendered store, and no deployed event since it last changed deployed Created, and deployed since, or with no rendered store retired Status retired, or a revoked event

Each report row carries its progress and a next step: where to create it, the command and how to install it in each store; or how each rendered store is written; then the event to record. A planned credential with a created event is assessed like an active one, so credentials can be made ahead of their launch.

docs.title: Reach
docs.text: Exposes(id) follows dependsOn and reaches from a credential, and their links in turn, to every credential a holder can get: what a leak exposes in all. ExposedBy(id) follows them backwards: whose leak exposes this one. Cycles are allowed.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Assess(credential, record, now, warn) gives one state, the reason and the next date that matters.

Order State When 1 retired Status retired, or a revoked event 2 planned Status planned 3 unrecorded Active, with no created or rotated event 4 expired The expiry has passed 5 overdue scheduled, and the last rotation plus the interval has passed 6 expiring The expiry is within warn 7 due scheduled, and the rotation date is within warn 8 unknown-expiry on-expiry, with no expiry recorded 9 ok Otherwise

The default warning window is 30 days.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
All three are built from the same rows: each credential, its record, its assessment and its events. Each counts the credentials that need a person for at least one stage, those handled entirely by systems, and each stage's human and system counts, the scheduled rotations a person does in a year (the sum of 365 / interval), and how many a person rotates at the issuer's expiry. Each row lists what it exposes and what exposes it.

  • HTML: one file with no external requests. It holds the rows as JSON in a <script type="application/json"> element, written through html/template, and a short script draws the table. It offers a text search over ID, name, description and paths; filters for system, environment, kind, state, issuer, store, consumer, owner, sensitivity and tag, and by who does each stage; sortable columns; counts per state; the handling counts; and a detail panel per row with every attribute and the history. Light and dark themes follow the viewer's setting. The page is assessed at the start of a day (UTC) and records that date in a meta element, so a committed copy can be rebuilt from the same registry, events and date and compared byte for byte.
  • Markdown: a "by hand, by place" checklist of the credentials a person makes, grouped by issuer and account, each with its store; then a section per system with a table and the details of each entry, including how to install it in each store. It uses only the registry, never the time or the events, so a test can check a committed copy is current.
  • Plan: the management plan in Markdown: a summary (counts by status, system and environment, state and who does each stage); the launch checklist of what a person creates (planned, or active with nothing recorded), accounts first, then those of no one environment, then each environment in a given order and its systems in a given order, each credential after those it is built from, with where to create it, the command, how to install it in each store and the command that records it; the rotation calendar; the accounts' protections, ticked by verified events; and the credentials whose leak exposes the most, with what cannot be recovered and its backup.
  • Calendar: the rotation calendar as an iCalendar (RFC 5545) file: an all-day event per scheduled rotation (repeating at its interval) and per expiry, with a reminder before it, and the procedure, impact, console and record command in its description. Late items go on the report's date. Event IDs are stable, so a newer file updates the same events.
  • JSON: the rows with their assessments, for other tools.

The HTML page, the plan and the calendar depend on the time. Each records its date (a meta element, a comment, an X- property), which report.AsOf reads, so a committed copy can be rebuilt and compared.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
credspec validate
credspec status   [--fail-on expired,overdue] [--progress to-create,to-deploy] [--manual] [filters]
credspec report   --format html|markdown|plan|ics|json [-o file] [--as-of date]
                  [--months 12] [--environment-order prod,staging] [--system-order a,b] [--remind-days n]
credspec record   <id-or-pattern> <created|rotated|expires|deployed|verified|revoked> [--at] [--expires] [--by] [--note]
credspec export   [-o file]
credspec schema   registry|events [-o file]

The standalone command reads --registry (JSON) and --events. A host mounts the same tree with cli.New(cli.Options{Use, Registry, EventsPath}), where Registry is a function that builds the registry, for example from Go code. export writes a Go-built registry as JSON.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• No type has a field for a value, and no command reads one.
  • The HTML report escapes all registry text; the JSON element is written in a script data context, so </script> in a description cannot end it.
  • Reports name stores and paths. They are as sensitive as an inventory, and are kept with the registry, not published.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Unit tests for validation, the event log, every state and boundary, each report (including escaping), the schema's currency and the commands. No network.
